rv.q: Much the same might be said of Mr. Spector’s ambitious, challenging and altogether extraordinary play.
More than three hours of overlapping speech race along without our feeling the passage of time, even as nearly two decades of the characters’ lives go whizzing by.
It’s gorgeous, it’s terrible, and it feels profoundly true.

But, as heartfelt and skillfully performed as “Birthright” is, in its eagerness to become a healing ritual for the audience it dodges what Dahl, in an acid exchange in “Giant,” deems “the vexing bit.”

Jonathan Spector’s Birthright at MCC Theater is an overwhelming wallop of a play, encompassing America’s frayed relationship with Israel as well as the individual struggle to reconcile religious affiliation with personal ethics.
With any luck, “Birthright” will also make it to Broadway, and more quickly, because it’s an even better play and, at this juncture, a more important one.
For a play this scintillating, it's never too darn hot.
Not only is his taste in plays downright flawless, Bergman knows how to bring a comic, wry edge to even the most serious of subjects.
Like Spector's 'Eureka Day,' 'Birthright' combines highly detailed characters with a sharp feel for the social pressures of its moment.

With impressive craftsmanship, Spector and director Teddy Bergman employ their characters to simultaneously examine four different facets of our complex world as they move from youthful innocence to painful lessons learned.
This is a play that has a lot to say and entertainingly makes it go down easy.
You’ll want to stay in this world as long as possible.
The contradiction in their relationships — profound love and knotty disagreement, glibness and generosity — was really always part of their friendship.
But the result is an evening that ultimately feels overly cautious and disappointingly half-hearted.

Spector has crafted the best new play of the year, a drama that zeroes in on the specifics of 21st-century American Jewish identity while sketching how all of us strain under the weight of conflicting politics, religion, and personal dynamics.
The result is an engagingly complex play that's both relatable and timely, an early standout in this new theatrical season.
Jonathan Spector destroys all that cautiousness and timidity with his bold, ambitious and ultimately transcendent new play, Birthright, which, not mincing words, needs to move to Broadway ASAP.
Birthright is the play of the year.

cn.t: Spector's ambitious 3+ hour drama about six Jewish friends over 18 years earns widespread praise for its sharp dialogue, emotional depth, and fearless exploration of identity and Israel, though a few critics find it frustrating or overextended.

vr.q: I really did love birthright so much. I thought the cast was phenomenal.
Jewish or not, this is definitely a Broadway Ben must see.
